summary: An indologist and linguist, Wilhelm Rau studied at Leipzig under Friedrich Weller, Marburg under Johannes Nobel (PhD 1946–1949), and with Shanti Bhikshu Shastri. He was a professor at Frankfurt (1955) and Ordinarius at Marburg (1957–1988).

Working in linguistics and other fields, Wilhelm Scherer earned his PhD at Vienna and studied at Berlin under Haupt, Bopp, von Ranke, and Müllenhoff. He held chairs at Vienna (1868–1872), Strasbourg (1872), and Berlin (1877).

Wilhelm Schmidt, a scholar of linguistics and religious studies, studied at Berlin and Vienna. He directed the Anima Mundi Museum (1927) and Anthropos Institute (1931), and was a professor at Vienna (1925–1938) and Fribourg (from 1939).

A scholar of sinology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and linguistics, Wilhelm Schott studied at Giessen, Halle (PhD), and Berlin. He taught as a Privatdozent at Halle (1826) and was an apl. Professor at Berlin (1838–1884).

A linguist and indologist, Schulze studied at Berlin under Steinthal and Schmidt, and completed his PhD at Greifswald under Zimmer. He was a professor at Marburg (1892), Göttingen (1895), and Humboldt University of Berlin (1902–1932).

Wilhelm Siegling was a scholar of indology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and linguistics. He studied at Halle, Heidelberg, Leipzig, Greifswald, and Berlin, earning his PhD under Richard Pischel, and worked at the Ethnological Museum and Prussian Academy.
An indologist, Wilhelm Solf studied at Berlin under Weber, Göttingen under Kielhorn and Bechtel, Halle under Pischel (PhD), and Jena (Dr.iuris). He held a post at Kiel University.

A scholar of linguistics and other fields, Wilhelm Storck studied at Munich, Münster, Bonn, and Berlin, completing his PhD under Franz Bopp and Albrecht Weber. In 1862, he became an associate professor at the University of Münster.

A linguist and indologist, Streitberg studied at Münster, Leipzig (Dr. phil. under Brugmann, Leskien, Windisch, and Zarncke), and Berlin. He held professorships at Fribourg (1889–1898), Münster (1899–1909), Munich (1909–1920), and Leipzig (1920–1925).

Wilhelm Tomaschek worked in Iranian and Central Asian studies, historical geography, and linguistics. He studied at Vienna under Friedrich Müller and Franz Xaver Miklosich, later becoming professor of geography at Graz (1877–1881) and historical geography at Vienna (1885).

Wilhelm Vatke, a scholar of religious studies and philosophy, studied at Halle-Wittenberg, Göttingen, and Berlin between ~1825 and ~1830. He subsequently held a post at Humboldt University of Berlin from ~1834 to 1882.

Wilhelm Volck worked in religious studies, linguistics, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at Erlangen (PhD under Friedrich von Spiegel) and Leipzig, later holding professorships at Tartu (1864–1898), Greifswald (1898–1900), and Rostock (1900).

A linguist, Wilhelm Wackernagel studied at Humboldt University of Berlin under Karl Lachmann and August Boeckh (1824–1827). He taught at the Gymnasium am Münsterplatz and served as an Ordinarius at the University of Basel (1835–1869).

Wilhelm Wissmann was a linguist who earned his PhD at Humboldt University of Berlin under Wilhelm Schulze. He held academic posts at Freiburg (1940), Königsberg (1942), Humboldt University of Berlin (from 1945), and Munich (from 1953).

A scholar in philosophy and other fields, Wilhelm Wundt studied at Tübingen, Heidelberg, and Berlin. He held posts at the University of Zurich (1857), the University of Leipzig (1858), and Heidelberg University (1864).

Active in linguistics, indology, and philosophy, Wilhelm von Humboldt studied at Viadrina, Göttingen, and Jena under teachers including Heyne and Chézy. He served in the Prussian Ministry (1819) and held a post at Berlin (~1809–1810).
Wilhelm von Pochhammer worked in the fields of history, archaeology, and indology. Between 1910 and 1914, he pursued his studies at the universities of Freiburg, Marburg, Munich, and Bonn.

Will Sweetman is a scholar of religious studies and indology who completed his studies at Lancaster University (~1990–1993) and the University of Cambridge (~1994–1998). Around 2005, he became a professor at the University of Otago.

Will Tuladhar-Douglas works in religious and Buddhist studies and was educated at the University of Oxford. He served as Director of the Scottish Centre for Himalayan Research, lectured at Aberdeen, and is attested at Hamburg (2026).

Willard Gurdon Oxtoby worked in religious studies and Iranian/Central Asian studies, studying at Stanford, Princeton, and Harvard. He taught at McGill (1960–1964) and Yale (1966–1971), then held a professorship at Trinity College, Toronto (1971–1999).
